column1: epistemology-03|The stopped clock displays the actual time.|A true belief from any clock constitutes knowledge.|The reader knows the time.|The same clock would mislead at most other times.|Compare the clock against an independent clock at several times.|Reliability checks could prevent lucky true belief from being mistaken for knowledge.

epistemology-04|Two peers reach opposed conclusions from the same evidence.|Equally informed disagreement always requires equal confidence.|Both peers should suspend judgment.|One peer may have made an identifiable inferential error.|Have each reconstruct the inference without seeing the other's conclusion.|A transparent error check may justify asymmetric confidence.

epistemology-05|A belief improves motivation but is known to be false.|Practical benefits are sufficient for epistemic rationality.|The false belief is epistemically rational to retain.|A belief can help action while misrepresenting evidence.|Compare motivational outcomes while separately checking factual accuracy.|A useful strategy need not count as a warranted belief.

epistemology-06|A speaker's accent lowers their credibility in a meeting.|Accent alone is reliable evidence of testimonial inaccuracy.|The speaker deserves less credibility.|Accent may be unrelated to the reliability of this testimony.|Compare matched testimony with and without identifiable accent cues.|Removing irrelevant credibility cues may change whose evidence is heard.

epistemology-07|No observer reports the bird.|If the bird were present, observers would almost certainly report it.|The bird is probably absent.|Observers may miss a quiet bird in an inaccessible habitat.|Estimate detection rates through comparable blinded surveys.|Absence reports become informative only with adequate detection.

epistemology-08|Every offered reason can be questioned.|A reason is justified only if an unending chain is completed.|No belief can be justified.|A coherent or basic justification may not require an infinite chain.|Compare candidate stopping rules on concrete objections.|Different standards can resolve or relocate the regress without a decisive experiment.

epistemology-09|A recording conflicts with remembered dialogue.|An intact recording is more reliable than this memory.|The remembered account should be revised.|The recording may be edited or lack relevant context.|Check provenance and compare independent recordings or witnesses.|Revision may depend on source integrity rather than confidence alone.

epistemology-10|Ten reports copy one source.|The ten reports count as ten independent confirmations.|Confidence should increase as if ten independent sources agreed.|A single error can propagate unchanged through all ten reports.|Trace the reports to their original sources.|Source tracing may sharply reduce apparent evidential diversity.

epistemology-11|A cyclist succeeds but cannot explain balance verbally.|All knowledge must be articulable in propositions.|The cyclist lacks knowledge of balancing.|Competent performance may instantiate knowing how.|Compare performance across unfamiliar routes and requests for explanation.|Performance and verbal explanation may measure different capacities.

epistemology-12|A perfect simulation cannot be conclusively excluded.|Ordinary knowledge requires excluding every skeptical possibility.|No ordinary external-world knowledge is possible.|Knowledge may require ordinary reliable grounds rather than absolute certainty.|Specify what evidence could distinguish the proposed scenarios, if any.|An empirically indistinguishable possibility may leave practical evidence unchanged.

ethics-03|One rescue saves three people and another saves one at equal risk.|Saving the greater number is always the decisive moral consideration.|The rescue boat should save the three.|Special duties or fairness may constrain simple aggregation.|Specify equal-risk facts and compare impartial and duty-based reasons.|More lives may be saved while a rival duty remains contested.

ethics-04|Equally reckless actions have different accidental outcomes.|Moral blame depends solely on voluntary risk-taking.|The two drivers deserve equal blame.|Actual injury may generate distinct responsibilities even with equal culpability.|Separate judgments of culpability, repair and legal liability in matched cases.|Different kinds of responsibility need not move together.

ethics-05|A true statement is made to humiliate.|Truthfulness alone makes a speech act morally good.|The humiliating statement is morally good.|A truthful disclosure can be cruel and unnecessary.|Compare intention, context and foreseeable harm in matched disclosures.|Accuracy may coexist with avoidable humiliation.

ethics-06|A worker accepts danger without another viable job.|Any expressed acceptance is fully voluntary consent.|The employer is justified by consent alone.|Severe dependence may undermine meaningful refusal.|Assess available alternatives, information and options to exit.|Expanding alternatives may change what the worker actually accepts.

ethics-07|Moderate sacrifice could prevent serious harm far away.|Distance alone cancels duties of assistance.|There is no duty to assist the distant people.|Distance need not alter the importance of comparable suffering.|Compare feasibility and competing obligations across near and distant cases.|Distance may affect practical ability without settling moral standing.

ethics-08|Present comfort leaves dangerous waste for future people.|Only currently existing persons can have morally relevant claims.|Future harm imposes no present constraint.|Predictable future interests may matter without current claimants.|Estimate durable hazards and explicitly compare principles of intergenerational justice.|Long-term safeguards may reduce risk but cannot choose the moral principle alone.

ethics-09|Animals lose possible pleasant lives without experiencing pain.|Avoiding pain exhausts all morally relevant animal interests.|The practice raises no further animal-welfare objection.|Deprivation of future goods may matter independently of suffering.|Distinguish pain measures from lifespan and opportunities for positive experience.|A painless practice can still reduce future opportunities.

ethics-10|Stolen money is returned anonymously.|Restoring the financial amount fully repairs wrongdoing.|No further repair is owed.|Trust, opportunity costs and acknowledgment may remain damaged.|Identify losses and ask what restoration would address each without compelling forgiveness.|Financial restitution may leave relational harm unresolved.

ethics-11|Two patients have equal need but elicit unequal sympathy.|Felt sympathy should decide priority whenever resources are scarce.|The more sympathetic patient should receive priority.|Emotion can track familiarity rather than morally relevant need.|Compare a blinded needs assessment with sympathy-based allocation.|Emotional concern can motivate care while requiring impartial allocation constraints.

ethics-12|A person offsets emissions from a wasteful practice.|An equal net emissions balance fully justifies the practice.|The practice is justified by the offsets.|Offsets may be unreliable or leave distributive and exemplary effects.|Audit additionality, permanence and who bears burdens.|Even verified emissions compensation may leave non-carbon concerns.

metaphysics-03|A promise changes recognized obligations.|Only weighable objects exist in any meaningful sense.|Promises do not exist in any meaningful sense.|Institutional entities may be real without being material objects.|Specify the explanatory and social consequences of removing promise practices.|Social dependence can explain effects without reducing existence to weight.

metaphysics-04|A spark, oxygen and dry wood jointly enable a fire.|Only the most salient enabling condition is genuinely causal.|Oxygen is not a cause of the fire.|Changing oxygen can prevent ignition while other factors remain fixed.|Compare interventions on oxygen, dryness and spark under controlled conditions.|Different explanatory questions can select different causal contrasts.

metaphysics-05|Deliberation feels open to alternatives.|An experience of alternatives establishes metaphysical indeterminism.|The future is metaphysically unsettled.|A deterministic process might include deliberation and uncertainty.|Distinguish predictions about experienced choice from claims about physical determinism.|Psychological observations may not decide the metaphysical thesis.

metaphysics-06|Objects are described through relations.|Relations require independently individuated relata.|A fully relational ontology is impossible.|Structural accounts may individuate objects by their relational roles.|Compare whether rival descriptions distinguish symmetric and asymmetric structures.|A structural model can clarify commitments without settling all ontology.

metaphysics-07|Different people prove the same theorem.|Convergent proof requires mind-independent mathematical objects.|Numbers exist independently of minds.|Shared inferential rules could explain convergence without that ontology.|Compare what Platonist and formalist explanations predict about proof practice.|Agreement in proof may underdetermine metaphysical explanation.

metaphysics-08|Removing one grain usually leaves a heap.|Any one-grain removal preserves heaphood without exception.|Repeated removal can never eliminate a heap.|The empty collection is not ordinarily a heap.|Apply candidate boundary rules and compare borderline cases.|A usable threshold need not establish a sharp natural boundary.

metaphysics-09|The model contains a first moment of time.|Every cause must be temporally earlier than its effect.|The beginning of time cannot have a cause.|Causation might be conceived as non-temporal dependence.|Specify whether each proposed cause is a temporal event or grounding relation.|A conceptual distinction may make the question intelligible without empirical confirmation.

metaphysics-10|An explanation ends at a basic fact.|A successful explanation must explain every fact without remainder.|This explanation necessarily fails.|Some explanatory standards permit brute facts or basic laws.|Compare what rival standards explain and what they assume.|Stopping points can be assessed without pretending an infinite regress was completed.

metaphysics-11|Two beings have exactly the same qualitative properties at an instant.|Qualitative identity entails numerical identity.|There is only one being.|Distinct locations or histories may individuate qualitative duplicates.|State which relational and historical properties are included in the description.|Changing the individuation criterion changes what counts as a duplicate.

metaphysics-12|Objects reflect light with stable physical dispositions.|Color is exhausted by those dispositions.|Color exists independently of perceivers.|Phenomenal color may depend on perceiver and illumination.|Compare stable spectra with differing perceiver reports under controlled illumination.|Physical stability may coexist with differences in experienced color.

logic-03|An argument reaches a true conclusion from an irrelevant premise.|A true conclusion guarantees a valid inference.|The argument is valid.|The premise could be true while a similarly formed conclusion is false.|Construct an interpretation with true premises and a false conclusion.|Countermodels can separate lucky truth from valid support.

logic-04|A broken device produces a flashing warning and the warning flashes.|Only a broken device can produce a flashing warning.|The device is broken.|Testing mode may flash the same warning.|Enumerate other warning causes and test the device independently.|A successful diagnosis requires more than affirming the consequent.

logic-05|A service is free of monetary price.|Anything free of price is free of obligations.|The service carries no obligations.|An unpriced service can require data or contractual duties.|List monetary charges and nonmonetary obligations separately.|Clarifying the two senses may reveal an equivocation.

logic-06|Some popular policies are unjust.|A property of some popular policies belongs to every popular policy.|All popular policies are unjust.|One just popular policy defeats the universal inference.|Construct a set containing both just and unjust popular policies.|A finite countermodel can refute the purported entailment.

logic-07|An opponent's wording admits two readings.|The weakest available reading is the right target for criticism.|One should attack that weakest reading.|The opponent may explicitly endorse the stronger reading.|Ask for confirmation of premises before evaluating their inferential connection.|Charitable reconstruction can improve relevance without granting truth.

logic-08|A source claims that it is reliable.|A source's own assurance suffices to establish reliability.|The source is reliable.|An unreliable source can make the identical assurance.|Compare the source's claims with independently checkable outcomes.|External checks may break the circular dependence.

logic-09|A household and a city both manage budgets.|Every borrowing rule appropriate to a household applies to a city.|A city should never borrow.|Public investment and taxation powers may defeat the analogy.|Compare relevant institutional capacities and long-term financing outcomes.|Relevant disanalogies can weaken the inference without proving all borrowing good.

logic-10|A proposed rule change creates one exception.|One exception inevitably causes every later exception.|The rule will necessarily collapse.|Enforcement criteria may block later steps.|Specify each transition and look for mechanisms or counterexamples.|A supported risk claim can be weaker than inevitability.

logic-11|A critic behaves inconsistently with their stated principle.|Hypocrisy makes every argument by that critic unsound.|The critic's argument is unsound.|A hypocrite can state a valid argument with true premises.|Evaluate premises and inference without the speaker's identity.|Character and argument validity can receive separate assessments.

logic-12|A debate presents surveillance and insecurity as the only options.|No policy can combine privacy protections with effective security.|Total surveillance is necessary for security.|Targeted safeguards may occupy an excluded middle ground.|Enumerate feasible intermediate policies and compare threat models.|A third option can defeat the framing without automatically being optimal.

mind-03|A machine imitates human conversation convincingly.|Convincing conversation is sufficient for understanding.|The machine understands.|A behavioral match may leave mechanisms or phenomenal properties unsettled.|Specify behavioral and mechanistic criteria, then test novel transfer tasks.|New tests may distinguish capacities while consciousness remains disputed.

mind-04|A person knows physical descriptions but has never felt a sensation.|Propositional physical knowledge includes every form of experiential acquaintance.|First sensation can add no kind of knowledge.|Acquaintance or practical recognition may differ from new propositional facts.|Separate factual reports, recognitional abilities and first-person acquaintance.|An observed learning difference need not immediately establish dualism.

mind-05|A person reliably retrieves information from a notebook.|Reliable external retrieval constitutes a component of cognition.|The notebook is part of the memory system.|A causal aid need not be a constitutive part of a mind.|Compare availability, trust and integration with familiar memory processes.|Functional integration can be studied while the constitutive boundary is debated.

mind-06|A driver performs familiar actions while attending elsewhere.|Every successful action requires conscious awareness of its details.|The driver is consciously aware of every action.|Automatic performance may proceed without reportable awareness.|Compare attention, later reports and performance under interruption.|Performance alone may not reveal the structure of awareness.

mind-07|Similar bodily arousal is experienced as fear and excitement.|Bodily arousal alone fixes emotional identity.|The two experiences must be the same emotion.|Interpretation and context may distinguish emotions.|Hold arousal similar while varying context and collect cautious reports.|Context-sensitive reports can challenge a simple arousal-only account.

mind-08|A bodily change alters how the environment is understood.|Cognition is independent of bodily capacities.|The bodily change should not affect cognition.|Action possibilities can shape perception and practical understanding.|Compare task strategies before and after changes in bodily affordances.|Embodied changes may alter cognition without proving every strong embodiment thesis.

mind-09|A person leaves after judging a room unsafe.|A reason cannot be both normative justification and causal explanation.|The safety judgment cannot play both roles.|One event may admit distinct causal and normative descriptions.|Distinguish whether the judgment motivated departure from whether it was warranted.|Causal efficacy and justificatory force may come apart or coexist.

mind-10|An actor offers a sincere reason while another motive may operate.|Any unrecognized motive eliminates agency entirely.|The actor has no agency.|Partial awareness may still permit control and reason-responsive action.|Compare opportunities for reflection and behavioral control without inferring hidden motives as facts.|Evidence of mixed motivation need not show total loss of agency.

mind-11|Two successors copy a prior person's mental state.|Matching psychological state uniquely fixes numerical identity.|Both successors are numerically the original person.|Numerical identity cannot ordinarily branch into two distinct persons.|Separate continuity, identity and practical responsibility in a branching case.|Different survival relations may preserve different concerns.

mind-12|An empathic observer closely understands another's pain.|Accurate understanding makes an experience numerically the same event.|The observer has the sufferer's very pain.|Similar content need not erase distinct subjects or occurrences.|Compare reported content and causal location without claiming direct access to another subject.|Shared understanding can coexist with distinct first-person ownership.

politics-03|A majority votes to silence a minority.|Majority approval is sufficient for every restriction's legitimacy.|The restriction is legitimate.|Basic liberties may constrain what a majority may authorize.|Compare a rights-based justification with the procedure's fairness and effects.|A valid vote may leave substantive legitimacy unsettled.

politics-04|Residents receive identical amounts despite different needs.|Identical shares suffice for distributive justice.|The distribution is just.|Equal resources may leave unequal basic capabilities.|Assess needs and consequences under equal-share and needs-sensitive allocations.|Outcome differences can inform but not settle the chosen conception of justice.

politics-05|Inherited wealth increases influence over political decisions.|Legitimate ownership always licenses unrestricted political influence.|The unequal influence needs no further justification.|Political equality may impose constraints independent of property rights.|Compare access and influence mechanisms under alternative institutional rules.|Reducing wealth-linked access may alter representation while tradeoffs remain.

politics-06|An employer holds unchecked power but does not interfere.|Freedom consists only in actual noninterference.|The dependent worker is fully free.|Arbitrary power may constitute domination without current interference.|Compare exit, appeal and legal protections in otherwise similar workplaces.|Institutional safeguards may change dependence even when observed interference is zero.

politics-07|Speech contributes to hostility and raises a public concern.|Any harmful effect is sufficient to justify restricting expression.|The speech should be restricted.|Broad restrictions may suppress legitimate criticism or exceed proportionality.|Specify evidence of harm, narrower alternatives and procedural safeguards.|A narrower remedy may reduce harm with less suppression.

politics-08|Protesters openly violate a law they judge unjust.|Sincere disagreement alone justifies breaking any law.|The civil disobedience is justified.|Sincerity alone cannot distinguish responsible protest from arbitrary preference.|Compare proportionality, public justification and available lawful remedies.|Justification may depend on more than conviction or legal compliance.

politics-09|Admission may protect people while straining public services.|Any strain on services defeats all duties to admit people in danger.|The country has no duty to admit them.|Serious threats and feasible redistribution may outweigh manageable burdens.|Estimate capacities and alternatives while making the moral weights explicit.|Capacity planning can inform but not determine the scope of obligation.

politics-10|Uniform institutional rules disadvantage one group.|Identical formal treatment guarantees neutrality.|The institution is neutral.|Background conditions may make a uniform rule systematically exclusionary.|Compare access and burdens while considering rival definitions of neutrality.|Unequal effects may require explanation without automatically proving intent.

politics-11|An institution benefits from a historical injustice.|Only direct perpetrators can owe any reparative duty.|The institution owes no repair.|Continuing benefits or inherited institutional obligations may ground responsibility.|Trace benefits, continuing harms and candidate remedies without presuming individual guilt.|Institutional duties may differ from personal culpability.

politics-12|A platform controls visibility of public arguments.|Political power exists only in formal governmental office.|The platform has no political power.|Agenda-setting can influence collective decisions outside office.|Audit recommendation and moderation effects under transparent comparison conditions.|Control over attention may be politically important despite private ownership.
